newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - EU warns against BA/AA slot-selling.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU warns against BA/AA slot-selling.

text.p: European Union sources warned on Monday that the European Commission still had "serious doubts" about whether to clear the alliance between American Airlines and BA, adding that recent suggestions of slot-selling made things worse.

"Selling slots is not something we can accept. It's not legal," one source said, referring to a British government statement that it would clear the alliance if the two companies met certain conditions including giving up 168 landing slots at London Heathrow airport.
British Airways responded that it would divest itself of slots only "on the basis of fair market value".
Landing and take-off rights are particularly valuable assets especially at congested airports such as London Heathrow, Paris Orly and Frankfurt.

EU rules forbid companies to trade slots, requesting instead that unused rights be made available to other carriers especially newcomers. But the Commission is aware of the existence of a secondary market for slots and is expected to regulate it.

In the alliance between BA and American Airlines, the EU sources said the companies should give the slots away rather than sell them. They also suggested that 168 slots was not enough to compensate for the alliance's possible threat to competition.
British Airways and the British government strongly contest that the Commission has competence for vetting the transatlantic link-up announced earlier this year despite public co-operation pledges.
But the EU sources said the deal affects Union territory as a whole -- not just U.S.-Britain routes -- and that EU legislation was appropriate.

"We have our own jurisdiction and we are going to apply it," one source said. The Commission is making particular use of articles 85 and 86 of the treaty of Rome which ban anti-competitive practices and abuse of dominant position.
Article 89 also enables it "to take appropriate measures" to end such infringements.
European lawyers and airline analysts expect the European courts may have to solve the issue.

"Several airlines have raised the issue. My own private view is that it could go to court," said Andre Clodong, a Brussels-based aviation consultant. Besides the BA-American link, the Commission is reviewing five other transatlantic airlines link-ups.

In October, the Commission sent BA and AA a so-called "statement of objections" outlining its concerns about the deal. The companies are expected to reply by January, after which the Commission could organise a hearing with all interested parties.

EU sources noted that on certain British-U.S. destinations the companies would control a large proportion of the passenger traffic -- for example, 83 percent on the London-Chicago route and 78 percent on the London-New York Kennedy Airport route, the sources said.
